title: A Bad Deal with Saudi Arabia
author: Mel Gurtov
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Donald_Trump_in_Saudi_Arabia_May_13_2025_7-680x453.jpg)

Photograph Source: The White House - Public Domain

**A Deal Without Safeguards**

The Trump administration has approved a deal with Saudi Arabia under which the
US will provide the material and technical capacity for that country to build
a nuclear power plant. The deal, said to last 30 years, gives US nuclear
energy companies, specifically Westinghouse and its reactor, a unique role in
providing for the civilian nuclear program. The next step would be to allow
the Saudis to engage in nuclear enrichment while ensuring that they cannot
build a bomb.

“The agreement could help revitalize the U.S. nuclear industry, strengthen
U.S.-Saudi ties and deny Russia and China a strategically important role in
the Saudi nuclear program,” said Robert Einhorn, a former senior State
Department official who advised both Republican and Democratic administrations
on nonproliferation issues. “But unless it contains adequate constraints,
including on enrichment, it could increase nuclear proliferation risks in the
Middle East and beyond,” Einhorn added.

Yes, “adequate constraints.” So far the administration has not been clear
about technical constraints though, as I will mention shortly, it has
belatedly imposed political conditions. Will Saudi Arabia be able to enrich
uranium on its own? Trump said no, after the deal was signed, while
administration officials who are privy to the agreement
[admitted](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/23/us/politics/saudi-nuclear-deal-
israel.html) it could happen. The Saudis may be thinking that since Iran
insists on the sovereign right to enrich uranium, why shouldn’t we?

**The Proliferation Danger**

That leads to other questions. Will the Saudis sign and ratify the Nuclear
Nonproliferation Treaty (NPT)? Will their nuclear facilities be subject to
international inspection by the International Atomic Energy Agency? What is to
stop Saudi Arabia from taking off on its own at some point and dispensing with
safeguards in the name of national security? There are precedents for doing
so. North Korea pulled out of the NPT in order to accelerate a nuclear weapons
program in total secrecy. India, Israel, and Pakistan have nuclear weapons and
no safeguards.

No matter how strong the safeguards on enrichment may be, if the deal goes
through—it is subject to Congressional review—it is bound to lead
[other](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/22/world/middleeast/us-saudi-arabia-
nuclear-deal.html) Middle East countries, such as Syria, to explore their
nuclear options. And for Israel, the prospect of a Saudi bomb unconstrained by
outside inspection would be a nightmare—essentially, another Iran. That might
prompt Israel to increase its nuclear weapon arsenal, which currently stands
at about 90 warheads, and change its nuclear doctrine in ways that further
destabilize the Middle East strategic picture.

**The Unlikely Quid Pro Quo**

Not long ago, prospects for such a deal seemed remote since the US required
that Saudi Arabia recognize Israel, and in return Palestinians would obtain a
clear path to statehood. When Trump announced this deal, he said nothing about
any requirement of the Saudis.

But after several members of Congress raised objections to the deal, Trump
said the agreement was “totally subject to” Saudi Arabia establishing
diplomatic relations with Israel under the 2020 Abraham Accords, which
normalized Israel’s relations with four Arab countries: the UAE, Bahrain,
Morocco, and Sudan. Was that an afterthought? Does “subject to” mean a legal
or a political obligation? Israel wants Saudi recognition, but surely not a
Saudi bomb or Palestinian statehood.

Karoline Leavitt, the administration’s spokesperson,
[said](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/07/23/us/trump-
news#section-518800265): “If they [Saudi Arabia] don’t join the Abraham
Accords, the deal is off.” But she didn’t say that the US would pursue a path
to Palestinian statehood as part of the deal—the very reason most Arab and
Muslim nations have refused to join the Accords.

The Saudis have to be stunned by Trump’s turnabout. As reported by David
Sanger in the New York Times, “Aaron David Miller, a former U.S. diplomat with
long experience in the Mideast, said that Mr. Trump again ‘alienated the
Saudis, delighted Benjamin Netanyahu and gave Iran strong talking points as to
why cutting deals with the US is a fool’s errand, bound to be betrayed.’” They
are not alone. As the Times is reporting, the UAE government, which has
defense and economic ties with Israel, has lost some of its initial enthusiasm
for the Abraham Accords it signed. “Uncertainty about the future of the
accords points to how Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran has risked
further undermining his signature policy achievement in the region. Across the
region, his pledge in recent months to expand the accords, including trying to
use them as a framework for a deal with Iran, have largely been met with
incredulity.”

**Scratch the Deal**

Both Saudi Arabia and the UAE are pressing Trump to end the war. The US bases
there have been among Iran’s main missile targets. The Houthis’ intervention
has further complicated matters for the Saudis. They, the UAE, and other US
partners in the region are baffled by Trump’s erratic swings between
escalation and pauses, and his seeming inability to find an exit ramp. Even
[Iran’s leaders](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/01/world/middleeast/us-iran-
war-strategy.html) are said to “have become intensely pessimistic about what
diplomacy with the Trump administration can achieve.” They have good reason,
dating back to the 2015 nuclear deal, not to trust that Trump will actually
fulfill the US part of any bargain.

Yet here is Trump pandering to the autocrat in Riyadh, Mohamad bin Salman, the
man who authorized the murder of the Washington Post journalist Jamal
Khashoggi, who only on occasion supports US energy policy, and who probably
influenced Trump to start a bombing campaign against the Houthis in 2025. Why?
Evidently in order to sell the Saudis more arms as well as nuclear
technology—and, no doubt, stay in the monarchy’s good graces for future real
estate deals.

Even putting aside this transaction between two unreliable and faithless
leaders, providing Saudi Arabia with nuclear technology is a bad deal that
should never have been offered. It is full of holes on enrichment, runs an
unacceptable risk of nuclear proliferation, and while good for Israel, will do
nothing to help the Palestinian people establish their own country. The deal
demonstrates a deplorable lack of foresight by Trump and his advisers in their
willingness to trade extraordinary policy and strategic gifts for nothing that
is in the human interest.
